claims.text: Controlled thermal aging combined with mechanical loading induces nanoscale elemental segregation at grain boundaries in initially homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary segregation produces localized nanoscale clusters.
The localized clusters reduce interfacial cohesion.
Reduced interfacial cohesion promotes brittle behavior.
The alloy can remain macroscopically single-phase while nanoscale grain-boundary segregation and brittle behavior develop.
The proposed behavior is distinct from the extensive grain-boundary precipitation associated with conventional alloys.
Service-like high temperatures activate diffusion in the alloy.
Differential diffusion under service conditions produces local chemical inhomogeneities at grain boundaries.
Nanoscale grain-boundary clusters facilitate crack nucleation and brittle fracture by diminishing grain-boundary cohesion.
Thermally aged and mechanically loaded samples will have lower fracture toughness than a rapidly quenched, homogenized baseline.
Thermally aged and mechanically loaded samples will absorb less impact energy than the baseline.
Thermally aged and mechanically loaded samples will exhibit more nanoscale grain-boundary segregation than the baseline.
Rapid quenching after homogenization prevents grain-boundary segregation.
The proposed mechanism is active only when service temperatures and stresses are sufficient to activate diffusion.
At very low temperatures or under minimal loading, diffusion-driven segregation and the resulting brittleness are not expected to occur.
The magnitude of toughness loss and the extent of segregation depend on alloy composition and service conditions.
